WSJ "앨리스 황은 대외적 얼굴…실제 밀수망 핵심은 동업자 리밍" 젠슨 황 전 엔비디아 최고경영자(CEO)가 2024년 6월2일 대만 타이베이에서 열린 '컴퓨텍스 2024' 기조연설을 마친 뒤 중국인 여성 사업가 앨리스 황을 포옹하고 있다. / 사진=로이터 연합뉴스 미국 정부의 수출 통제를 피해 엔비디아의 인공지능(AI) 반도체를 중국으로 빼돌린 배후 인물로 젠슨 황 전 엔비디아 최고경영자(CEO)의 내연 상대가 아닌 그의 50대 중국인 동업자가 지목됐다. 논란이 된 업체가 활동을 중단한 뒤에도 관련 인물들이 새 법인을 세워 최신 칩을 계속 공급받고 있다는 정황도 포착됐다. 21일(현지시간) 월스트리트저널(WSJ)은 복수의 소식통을 인용해 엔비디아 AI 칩을 중국으로 밀반출하는 기업 네트워크의 핵심 운영자가 싱가포르에 거주하는 중국 국적의 리밍(52)이라고 보도했다. 그동안 대중국 칩 밀수 의혹을 받아온 싱가포르 데이터센터 업체 메가스피드의 임원 앨리스 황(중국명 황러)은 대외적인 얼굴 역할을 맡았으며, 실제 주요 의사결정과 막후 운영은 리밍이 주도했다는 설명이다. 리밍은 엔비디아 칩 우회 수출 의혹과 관련해 2025년 2월 싱가포르에서 사기 혐의로 기소됐으며, 현재 보석으로 풀려나 싱가포르 주재 중국대사관 인근 고급 빌라에 거주하고 있다. 싱가포르 검찰은 리밍이 자신의 현지 법인 '럭셔리에이트 유어 라이프'에서 사용할 것처럼 미국 공급업체를 속여 엔비디아 칩 탑재 서버를 사들인 뒤, 말레이시아를 거쳐 확인되지 않은 제3의 장소로 빼돌렸다고 보고 있다. 당시 공소장에는 여러 기업이 포함됐으나 메가스피드는 빠졌다. 소식통에 따르면 리밍은 기소 이전부터 앨리스 황과 그의 남편 캉웨이와 함께 일했다. 부부가 2021년 설립한 클라우드 컴퓨팅 합작사 '센추리 룽텅'에서 리밍은 2023년 1월 기준 최고전략책임자(CSO)로 활동했다. 이후 조 바이든 행정부가 엔비디아 반도체의 중국 수출을 제한하자 세 사람은 중국 고객사에 칩을 공급하기 위해 동남아시아에 협력사 망을 구축하기 시작했다. 이들은 중국 게임사의 싱가포르 법인을 인수해 메가스피드로 사명을 바꾸고, 알리바바를 핵심 고객으로 내세워 2023년 11월 엔비디아 클라우드 파트너 지위를 확보했다. 최신 칩을 우선 구매할 수 있는 자격을 얻은 뒤 말레이시아로 서버를 들여와 알리바바에 합법적인 역외 컴퓨팅 파워를 제공하는 한편, 일부 서버는 미국 수출 통제를 위반해 상하이 기술기업 '센추리 리퉁'으로 보냈다. 센추리 룽텅은 2024년까지 센추리 리퉁의 주요 주주였다. 미국과 싱가포르 당국의 조사가 이어지자 엔비디아는 2025년 6월 메가스피드를 내부 '판매 금지' 명단에 올렸다. 앨리스 황은 같은 해 8월 퇴사했고, 싱가포르 당국은 그를 조사한 뒤 출국을 허용하면서 재입국을 금지했다. 메가스피드는 사실상 활동을 멈췄지만, 운영진의 사업은 다른 법인을 통해 이어지고 있는 것으로 파악됐다. 소식통들에 따르면 메가스피드 운영팀은 지난해 '노바게이트 클라우드'라는 새 회사를 설립했다. 노바게이트는 웹사이트에서 자사가 엔비디아 클라우드 파트너로서 최신 '블랙웰' 칩을 갖춘 데이터센터를 최소 2곳 운영하고 있다고 밝히고 있다. WSJ가 확인한 선적 기록에 따르면 노바게이트 말레이시아 법인은 올해 1~5월 블랙웰 칩이 탑재된 하드웨어를 최소 3억달러어치 반입했다. 공매도 업체 컬퍼 리서치 역시 지난 5월 보고서에서 두 회사의 웹사이

items.fullText: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs NVIDIA and Microsoft expand tools for enterprises to customize AI models and deploy applications across cloud and local infrastructure. NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. items.fullText: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now Systems from ASUS, Dell and MSI are now available — with more from Acer, GIGABYTE, HP and Microsoft on the way — bringing RTX acceleration and up to 128GB of unified memory to local AI, development and creative workflows. November 18, 2026 by Justin Walker 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC. With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work. Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops. Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC. A Windows PC Built for Local AI As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks. NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 16TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. items.fullText: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future Over two decades running the most complex manufacturing on the planet, NVIDIA operations chief Deb Shoquist has required three things of every supply chain partner: extreme technical skill, unshakeable trust and a willingness to always try something new. November 16, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades. Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago. For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it. Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow. To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient. Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale. “Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.” Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. Across rack, scalable unit and pod configurations, the network maintains the same throughput as conventional pluggable optics. Delivering Power Efficiency and Resiliency at Scale Improving power efficiency and resiliency matters because the network sits at the center of AI factory productivity. In a large training job, one interrupted link can stall thousands of GPUs. With agentic inference, one network disruption can introduce cascading latency effects on many agents. Every interruption costs time, and every watt spent on networking is a watt not available for compute. NVIDIA Photonics addresses both power efficiency and resiliency. By replacing pluggable transceivers with co-packaged optical engines on the switch package, it delivers up to 5x better power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. items.fullText: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing Quantum hardware developers, software providers and supercomputing centers are adopting the community-built Slurm workloads manager and the NVIDIA quantum platform to integrate quantum processors, design future systems and develop scientific applications. November 16, 2026 by Sam Stanwyck 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors. Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction. In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob , IBM , IQM , Pasqal , Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 Beating the Bottleneck Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology. The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems. The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 Bringing Black Holes Into Focus Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process. With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the cuPhoton Toolkit , black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes. By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time. The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact NVIDIA DGX Spark system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull. items.fullText: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing Over two decades, CUDA, the platform that turned GPUs into the engine of modern science, has advanced Nobel Prize-winning research and more. November 16, 2026 by Brett Murray 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI. CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today. At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do. From SC06 to SC26 NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more. In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research , accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films . Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack. As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design. The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps. “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck , vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.” Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing w

GeForce NOW will bring the action to supported PCs, Macs, handhelds and other devices, with game downloads and updates handled in the cloud.
